newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania leader admits mistakes on pyramid schemes.
newsitem.headline: Albania leader admits mistakes on pyramid schemes.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha admitted mistakes on Saturday in his handling of a scandal over failed pyramid investment schemes that has sparked a month of anti-government protests and riots.
But Berisha said sternly that responsibility also lay with those who had chosen to put hundreds of millions of dollars into the high-interest schemes -- and lost everything.

Addressing a meeting of selected supporters, he stressed that the state had no intention of reimbursing the hundreds of thousands of Albanians who lost their savings and often sold valuables or property to invest in the schemes.
"We will not take this debt on our shoulders. No democratic government would do this. It would be cheating, printing money to pay and creating hyperinflation," he said.

Berisha acknowledged that many Albanians were now homeless because they had sold their houses to join a national frenzy of pumping money into pyramid schemes which paid interest of 60 percent or more a month.
Bankers estimate $1 to $2 billion may have been poured into the fraudulent schemes -- five of which have gone bust over the past month.
Protests and riots have swept the country since January when the schemes began to fall. Several people have died and hundreds have been injured or arrested.
Berisha pleaded that the government had been naive and was new to democracy and capitalism. He appealed to all parties to join in trying to sort out the mess.
But in a thinly veiled reference, he then accused the main opposition Socialist Party -- the former Communists -- of trying to exploit the confusion for political advantage.

"Today, at a time when hundreds of thousands of Albanians are suffering from losses in pyramid schemes, a minority ... wants to turn this big but not irreparable loss into a a real national tragedy," he said.

To rousing applause from his audience, Berisha said there was no question of early elections over the scandal and dodged questions about whether the right-wing government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi would resign.
Albania, Europe's poorest country, emerged from 45 years of strict isolation and Stalinism in 1990 when Communism fell and democracy was established.
Berisha acknowledged the ruling Democratic Party, in power since 1992, was slow to raise a warning but he said this was because the government, like the public, was new to free market realities.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned the government last October that the schemes must be brought under control, he said.
But he added that any warning would have been countered by pyramid scheme managers raising interest rates even higher to suck in more money.
"At the time, who would the public have believed: our warnings or their higher interest rates?" he asked. The meeting erupted in cheers and applause.
Berisha, in his most extensive explanation of the crisis, dished out a warning to officials of his Democratic Party and others in the countryside.

He said that some members of the Democratic Party had posed inappropriately with managers of pyramid schemes during general elections last year. Such politicians should apologise, he said, and if any wrongdoing was found they would be held responsible.
